newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela film opens battle to portray his life.
newsitem.headline: Mandela film opens battle to portray his life.

text.p: The world premiere of a big-screen documentary about Nelson Mandela at the weekend opens the battle among film-makers to be the best at telling his remarkable story.

"Mandela" traces his life from boyhood and ritual circumcision in his remote rural home, through political agitation and three decades in jail and up to his 1994 inauguration as South Africa's first black president.
It ends with the divorcee -- now 78 and gradually handing over power to his chosen successor, Thabo Mbeki -- looking ahead calmly to his own death.
The film presents a lively history of the anti-apartheid struggle, mixed with personal anecdotes from Mandela himself and those close to him, including his two ex-wives Evelyn and Winnie.
Any feature-length documentary about a living leader -- this is the first on Mandela -- seems bound to boost his almost superhuman image.

But Island Pictures called their film "a means to an end" for the man who in 1990 said his hardest task in adjusting to life outside jail would be "getting people to see me as a human being, not as a messiah or a demi-god".
They say it is Mandela's only official film biography.

But some critics said the film was still too impersonal despite director Jo Menell's unprecedented access to Mandela. He let the crew film him shaving and being told off by his cook and he took them to his childhood home.

"It could do with many more intimate moments, such as when Mandela speaks movingly of his parents, discusses impishly with aides the dress code for his inauguration and begins his day by making his own bed," Monday's Star newspaper said.
The documentary, produced by "Silence of the Lambs" director Johnathan Demme and boiled down to two hours from 300 hours of footage, goes on general release in South Africa from Friday.
Its subject matter, the whole life of one of the world's most revered leaders, is identical to a second film being planned by South African director Anant Singh.
Mandela sold Singh the exclusive rights to dramatise his best-selling autobiography, "Long Walk to Freedom", earlier this year. Filming of the $10-million project starts next year.
A third production, backed by U.S. television network Showtime and starring American actor Sidney Poitier as Mandela, is set for TV and cinema release this year.

That film hones in on Mandela's crucial negotiations with then-president F.W. de Klerk -- played by Michael Caine -- and other parties which brought about South Africa's remarkable transformation to democracy in 1994.

Menell's documentary, accompanied by a soundtrack of much of the best of South African music, closes before the latest chapter in Mandela's private life, his romance with former Mozambican first lady Graca Machel, became public.

Instead it paints a picture of a somewhat lonely elderly man looking back at his life, knowing he has achieved his historic life-long goal and that his role in South Africa's future is drawing to a close.
"Death is something inevitable," Mandela says. "When a man has done what he considers his duty for his country he can rest for eternity. I believe I have done that."
